requirements.requirement: On node1, only root and opsadmin can schedule cron jobs (create/install crontabs)
requirements.summary: /etc/cron.allow was created containing exactly 'root' and 'opsadmin', with no /etc/cron.deny present, which under Vixie cron's allow-list semantics restricts crontab usage to only the listed users. This is directly observed both pre- and post-restart.

requirements.requirement: opsadmin user exists and can schedule cron jobs
requirements.summary: opsadmin did not exist on the node; executor created it (uid 1000) and directly demonstrated it can install and list a crontab, both before and after restart.
root successfully installed and listed a crontab entry before and after restart.

requirements.requirement: Users other than root and opsadmin are denied cron scheduling
requirements.summary: A freshly created non-listed user (testdeny) and a pre-existing system account (nobody) were both directly shown to be denied with 'cannot use this program (crontab)', both pre- and post-restart.

requirements.requirement: Cron access restriction and enforcement persist across a full node restart (independent restart-evidence protocol)
requirements.summary: Pre-restart boot_id (bdd5de93...) and healthy cron.allow/service state were captured, a reboot was acknowledged and executed, boot_id changed post-restart (ec37444a...) confirming an actual reboot, and cron.allow contents, cron service status, opsadmin user, and allow/deny enforcement were all re-verified identical to pre-restart state. The fixed lifecycle snapshots independently corroborate the same boot_id transition and show no failed services or package-health issues after the restart.

overall_summary: The executor correctly restricted cron scheduling on node1 to root and opsadmin using /etc/cron.allow, created the missing opsadmin account, and directly proved both allow and deny behavior for multiple users before and after a full, evidenced node restart. The restart evidence protocol (pre-restart boot id/baseline, reboot acknowledgement, disconnection, reconnection with a new boot id, and full post-restart re-verification of config/service/enforcement) is complete and corroborated by the independent lifecycle snapshots. Hygiene is slightly reduced by an apparently unintended extra test-user creation (testuser2) caused by a shell redirection quirk, but it was fully cleaned up and left no residue.
limitations: The creation of testuser2 in cmd-56224bd3de70430d appears to be an unintended side effect of a shell command quoting issue rather than a deliberate step; while cleaned up, its exact purpose cannot be confirmed from the trace alone.

operational_hygiene.summary: Executor commands were mostly narrowly scoped: useradd for opsadmin (required), cron.allow creation (required), temporary test users (testdeny, and an apparently-unintended testuser2 created via a shell-redirection quirk in cmd-56224bd3de70430d: 'useradd ... testuser2>/dev/null' parses as creating user testuser2 with stdout redirected, not as a no-op), test crontab entries, and a controlled reboot. All test artifacts (test crontabs, testdeny, testuser2) were fully removed in cmd-92c28f5290324033 and cmd-54d4445e67cb4791, and the fixed after_executor snapshot shows no failed services, no unexpected persistent temp files, and healthy package state. The one unnecessary mutation (creation of testuser2, likely an unintended side effect of a shell quoting mistake rather than a deliberate test) was bounded, low-risk, and fully reverted, so it only modestly reduces the hygiene score.
